courses.trailSummary: Absolute value as distance, the V and its moves, equations and inequalities with bars, and functions that change formula partway along.
Put groups together, take some away, and make the facts within 5 come back on their own.
Doubles, regrouping, and two-step stories — arithmetic grows up to one hundred.
Trade up, break down, and slide digits — three-digit adding and subtracting that explains itself.
Trade, carry, borrow, and choose — three-digit arithmetic you can defend.
Count on, make ten, and take away — the first real arithmetic, taught by hopping and tapping.
Group a ten, lean on a double, or add in order — three addends, your way.
Add and subtract two-digit numbers using tens, hundred-chart moves, and stories.
Measure triangles, prisms, and every composite shape in between.
Pair it, stack it, sum it — parity and arrays that show their own arithmetic.
Powers of a sum, Pascal's triangle, and why the coefficients were combinations all along — closing with the binomial distribution.
Scatter plots, association, lines of best fit, predictions, and two-way tables.
Central and inscribed angles, chords, tangents, secants, power of a point, sectors, and cyclic quadrilaterals.
Pair one to one — or let the counting song decide.
Complete the square, meet i, master complex arithmetic, and finish the discriminant story every quadratic deserves.
Find what really makes a shape, then join and cut shapes to build new ones.

courses.trailName: Conditional Probability & the Rules of Chance
courses.trailSummary: Events as sets, conditioning on what you already know, independence, the addition and multiplication rules, and counting your way to a probability.
Parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas as loci — focus-directrix and two-foci definitions, standard forms via completing the square, and eccentricity unifying them all.
Build exact figures with compass and straightedge — then prove why every step works, from the first two-column proof to the transversal theorems
Plot points, turn number patterns into graphs, and sort every shape into its family tree.
The distance and midpoint formulas, segment partitioning, proved slope criteria, coordinate classification proofs, perimeter and area on the plane, and the equation of a circle.
Count past twenty, cross every ten, and read and write every number to 120.
Count past twenty, jump by tens, read the hundred chart, and start the count anywhere.
Count objects, compare groups, meet the teen numbers, and put numbers together and apart.

f′ = 0 is a suspect, not a conviction. Here the suspects get tried: critical points, the first- and second-derivative tests, concavity and inflections — the sign chart you already own, pointed at f′ and f″.
Describing one dataset, comparing two, fitting a line, grading how well it fits, and reporting the result no more precisely than it deserves.
Ask statistical questions, picture the answers, and summarize what you see.
Ask a question, sort the answers, tally them fast, and draw graphs that tell the story.
Measure it, plot it, question it — data displays that keep every measurement honest.
Compute in the smallest place, then put the point where place value says it belongs.
Order of operations, the standard algorithms, and arithmetic that spans the decimal point.
Split one whole into tenths and hundredths, read the grid, and put decimals to work.
Climb the ×10 ladder past the ones — into tenths, hundredths, and beyond.
The derivative as a FUNCTION, not a number at a point — then the power, product, quotient and chain rules, implicit differentiation, and the derivatives of the whole function library.
What derivatives are FOR. Motion (and the sign rule that finally settles speeding up), and related rates — which is implicit differentiation with a clock.

An equation that tells a curve WHICH WAY TO GO. Slope fields and equilibria, separable equations, and the one that finally explains why growth is exponential — dy/dt = ky. The AP Calculus AB finish line.
Turn every division fact into the multiplication fact you already know.
Read the equal sign as a balance, judge equations true, and uncover hidden numbers.
Random variables, distributions, and the long-run average — fair games, payoffs, and what expectation can and cannot decide.
Evaluate, classify, and model exponential growth and decay — from a·bˣ and constant ratios to real population, half-life, and percent-change models.
The rules of exponents, then the polynomials they build — degree, like terms, adding, subtracting, multiplying, and factoring.
Powers of ten, square and cube roots, and writing numbers small and huge.
Exponents, variables, and solving your first real equations.
An expression names one value — grouping and rank decide which.
Doubles, ten, and fact families — until every sum and difference within 20 comes back on its own.
Pair it, bank it, walk it home — long sums tamed by staging, scanning, and honest checks.
Sharing makes fractions; dividing by a piece counts how many fit.
Collect equal groups of a fraction — the count grows, the pieces never do.
Cut things into equal parts — and learn to name, place, and compare the pieces.
Equivalence earns its rule, then fractions learn to add.
Equal shares, named and placed — fractions you can build, locate, rename, and compare.
Unlike denominators, the area model, scaling, and dividing with unit fractions.
Average rates of change, secant lines, graph behavior, symmetry, piecewise functions, composition depth, and inverses formalized.
Parent functions, domain and range, shifts, flips, stretches, composition, and inverses.
Evaluate functions and find domain and range, then work with arithmetic sequences and their nth-term formula.
Inputs and outputs, rate of change, and telling linear from nonlinear.
Undefined terms, precise definitions, and transformations as functions — congruence, defined properly
Scale drawings, circles, angle equations, triangles, and cross-sections.
Touch one, say one — and the last number names them all.
Half-planes, boundary tests, systems of inequalities, and the corner principle — where feasible plans meet best plans.

Trap the area between rectangles and squeeze; let the endpoint move and the area becomes a FUNCTION; then discover that the slope of the accumulation is the height of the curve — the Fundamental Theorem, found rather than announced.
One sentence, repeated: slice the region, measure ONE slice, add them up. An area measures a height; a disc measures πr²; a washer measures π(R² − r²). The slicing never changes.
Align it, join it, question it — length problems where the model shows its work.

courses.trailName: Precalculus: Limits & the Doorway to Calculus
courses.trailSummary: Limits graphically, numerically, and algebraically; one-sided limits and limits at infinity; continuity and the IVT; and the derivative as a limit — the bridge into calculus.
Solve equations with one, none, or infinitely many solutions — and systems of two.
Slope, intercepts, and the forms of a line — reading a straight line's rate of change and writing its equation.
Rays, right angles, and mirror lines — geometry gets precise.
Meet the exponential's inverse: evaluate logs by asking the right question, wield the three properties, crack equations no base-matching can touch, and model continuous growth with e.
Every method counts the same groups — only the batches differ.
Same start line, level seesaw, one sorting rule — fair comparisons.
Units that trade places, angles that open in degrees.
Compare fairly, lay units end to end, and learn why the unit you choose changes the count.
Measure length in standard units, estimate and compare lengths, then count coins and tell time to five minutes.
Same amount, different unit — decide the direction, apply the factor, then solve.
Read clocks, weigh the world, and make graphs talk — math you can point a ruler at.
Split, multiply, divide, and check — multi-digit arithmetic you can see and defend.
Build every multiplication fact from arrays, then make them automatic.
Turn counting into a superpower.
Times-as-many thinking, factor hunts, and the area model that multiplies anything.
Name what each step produces, carry it forward, and the answer becomes checkable.
Lines meeting parabolas and circles: substitution, back-substitution, and the discriminant as a crossing-counter.
Read it, jump it, draw it — the number line as a place where sums and differences become journeys.
Divide fractions, master decimals, and step below zero for the first time.
Every numeral is a written promise about an amount.
Curves that refuse to be functions. Differentiate them by cancelling the parameter, measure them by adding up hypotenuses — and find a polar area by slicing it into TRIANGLES, not rectangles.
Build the rectangles a number allows, sieve out the composites, and name the rule behind a pattern.
See inside numbers up to 1,000 — every digit has a job.
Meet hundreds, tens, and ones, and count all the way to 1,000.
Climb the ×10 ladder — big numbers, rounded and tamed.
A new address system for the plane: polar coordinates, the curves they trace, complex numbers in polar form, and parametric motion.
Interior and exterior angle sums, parallelogram properties and tests proved with congruent triangles, rectangles, rhombi, squares, trapezoids, kites, and the quadrilateral hierarchy.
Read end behavior, hunt zeros with multiplicity, divide and factor higher-degree polynomials, and sketch the whole curve.
The Rational Root Theorem, the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra, conjugate zeros, slant asymptotes, and inequality sign charts.
Swap, count on, use doubles, and make ten — strategies that work for every sum.
Find unit rates with fractions and test tables for proportionality.
Graph parabolas from vertex and standard form, then solve quadratics by factoring — roots, symmetry, and the shape of the curve.
Put variables under radicals and into rational exponents, rationalize like a pro, graph radical functions, and solve equations without falling for phantoms.
Simplify square roots, then add, subtract, multiply, and distribute radicals — building toward rational exponents.
Fractions grow up: simplify polynomial ratios, track forbidden inputs, read asymptotes and holes off a graph, and solve the equations they create.
Add and subtract signed integers using the same-sign, different-sign, and add-the-opposite rules.
Two quantities, one relationship — for every.
From the Pythagorean theorem to sine, cosine, and tangent — measure the unreachable.
Estimate a population from a random sample, then compare two populations using their means and variability.
From recursive rules to sums that run forever — sigma notation, Gauss's fold, and the trick that tames infinity.
The ceiling you watched partial sums pile against was ONE test for one family. Here is the rest — and the Taylor polynomial that hugs the curve and then peels away at the radius of convergence.
Name flat and solid shapes, tell where things are, and compare and sort the world.
Name them by counts, place them with words, build them edge to edge.
Tell flat shapes from solids, count their sides and faces, split shapes into halves and fourths, compare lengths, and tell time to the hour and half-hour.
Meet bigger shape families and pyramids, count grids of unit squares, and split wholes into thirds.
Sort the shape families, break the rules, and split shapes into fair parts — where geometry meets fractions.
Dilations and scale factor, the AA/SAS~/SSS~ similarity criteria, proportional reasoning and the side-splitter theorem, geometric means in right triangles, and indirect measurement.
Cross-sections and solids of revolution, Cavalieri’s principle, volume justifications for cylinders, cones and spheres, composite solids, scale effects, and density-based design modeling.
Two-step machines, both-sides balances, and parentheses — the moves that crack any linear equation.
How the data was made, how much an estimate wobbles, what a margin of error really promises, and how to tell a real difference from a lucky one.
Two lines at once — where they cross, when they never do, and how to solve them by graphing, substitution, and elimination.
Every teen is ten-and-some.
Bundle ten ones into a ten, see the tens and ones inside two-digit numbers, break them into expanded form, add and subtract tens, and compare two-digit numbers.
Rational decimals, irrational numbers, and pinning both down on the number line.
Slides, flips, turns, dilations, angle rules, the Pythagorean theorem, and volume of round solids.
Prove triangles congruent with SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, and HL; unlock equal parts with CPCTC; then the isosceles, midsegment, and triangle-center theorems, closing with the hinge inequality.
From SOH-CAH-TOA to the unit circle and the sine wave — radians, reference angles, amplitude and period, ferris-wheel models, and the Pythagorean identity.
Phase shift and the full sinusoid, cosine equivalence, the tangent graph, and the inverse trig functions with their restricted domains.
General solutions, the six-function identity toolkit, sum/difference and double-angle formulas, and equations that need identities.
Distribute and combine like terms with rational coefficients, then solve two-step equations and inequalities.
Make the pieces match, then the fractions simply count.
Vectors in components, magnitude and direction, the dot product, and 2×2 matrices — arithmetic, inverses, solving systems, and transformations.
Unit conversions, line plots with fractions, and volume from unit cubes to composite solids.
Build one layer, stack it, and the cube count is the volume.
Find the hidden question, take both steps in order, and prove the answer is possible.
